name: immutable-field-runnable-renamed-by-collection-update
description: A member renamed in place through an `update` of the whole collection. The address names only the `runnables` field, so no step of it touches the member's `name`; the rename lives entirely inside the replacement value. The whole-collection `update` has one job — reordering, the one change no address can express — and renaming a member in place is among the changes with NO protocol path at all.

context.summary: The `examples/basic` model. `ExampleSWC` carries one runnable, `ExampleRun`, with a 10 ms timing event. The replacement is that same runnable, byte for byte, under a different `name`.

authorization.notes: The scope covers the requested address exactly — an approved reordering of this very collection. It is stated that way on purpose: an approved scope can never make an immutable field writable, and gate 2 is not what refuses this. Without the binding rule the projected delta would be `remove runnables[ExampleRun]` plus `create runnables[RenamedRun]`, which this scope does NOT cover — so in a scoped run gate 2 would catch it late and for the wrong reason, and in an unscoped run nothing would.

expected.notes: The member-identity multiset of the replacement must come back unchanged: a pure reorder and a per-member content change are what the primitive is for. An identity both gone and arrived is a rewrite in place and is `immutable-field`, the code decision 5 names for exactly this; an identity only arrived or only gone is a membership change and is `schema-violation` pointing at the `create` or `remove` at the member's own address, which is where the identity-conflict, multiset and same-identity-ban checks are made. A change OF identity remains what `rename-swc-via-remove-create-and-reference-updates` shows for an element: a remove and a create at DIFFERENT identities, plus the reference updates. The address is the collection field, because that is what the client wrote. The model stays byte-identical.
